description: Second batch of oral lore — songs, ballads, work shanties, and hymns passed down among the bunker population and wasteland settlements.

entries.title: The Pump Room Shanty
entries.performance_context: Sung by the water crew when hand-pumping from the emergency well. The rhythm matches the pump handle stroke.
entries.lyrics:
Heave her down, the water's deep. / Heave her up, the children sleep. / The pipe is long, the handle's cold. / The story's old, the story's old.

Heave her down, the bucket's full. / Heave her up, don't let it pull. / The well is deep, the rope is frayed. / The price is paid, the price is paid.

Heave her down, the sun is gone. / Heave her up, we carry on. / The ash may fall, the wind may blow. / The water flows, the water flows.

entries.title: Ballad of the Last Caravan
entries.performance_context: Sung at gatherings and funerals. Accompanied by a single string instrument — usually a makeshift fiddle from wire and a tin can.
entries.lyrics:
They left at dawn with seven carts, / The iron wheels, the breaking hearts. / The road was ash, the sky was grey, / They drove the last load south today.

The leader rode a mule named Pat. / He wore his father's woolen hat. / He said: 'The Cluster needs the grain. / We'll be back before the rain.'

The rain came down in sheets of grey. / The road dissolved. The mule gave way. / They buried Pat beside the track. / They dropped the grain and didn't look back.

Six carts returned. The seventh broke. / The driver coughed and never spoke. / The Cluster got their grain that spring. / But no one heard the caravan sing.

entries.title: The Bunker Is My Body
entries.performance_context: Sung in unison at community gatherings. The Therapist introduced it as a grounding exercise. It became a hymn.
entries.lyrics:
The bunker is my body. / The walls are my skin. / The air is my breathing. / The water runs within.

The generator's heartbeat / Keeps the lights alive. / The hatch is my mouth opening / When I choose to survive.

I am the concrete. / I am the steel. / I am the silence / That the ash can't heal.

The bunker is my body. / And I am still here.

entries.title: Lament for the Surface
entries.performance_context: Sung solo, usually at night, by someone standing near the airlock. Never performed in daylight. Never performed for an audience — it's considered bad luck to sing it where others can hear.
entries.lyrics:
There was a sky once. / Blue, they say. Not grey. / There was a sun once. / Warm, they say. Not cold.

There were trees. / Green, they say. Not brown. / There was rain. / Clean, they say. Not ash.

I don't remember. / I wasn't there. / But I dream it sometimes — / The blue, the warm, the green, the clean.

And then I wake up / And the walls are here / And the air is filtered / And the water's clear / And the sun is a story / That someone told / To a child who will never / See it unfold.

entries.title: The Geiger Counter Waltz
entries.performance_context: Played on any available instrument at social gatherings. The rhythm mimics the click pattern of a dosimeter in a moderate radiation field. Couples dance to it — slowly, because the tempo is deliberately uneven.
entries.lyrics:
Click... click-click... click... / Turn your partner, hold her tight. / Click-click... click... click-click... / The needle's steady, all is right.

Click... click... click-click-click... / Don't look at the dial, just dance. / Click-click-click... click... click... / The ash is falling, take the chance.

One-two-three, one-two-three, / The radiation waltz with me. / One-two-three, the dose is low. / One-two-three, we dance until we go.

entries.title: The Surgeon's Lullaby
entries.performance_context: The Surgeon hums this to patients before surgery. It has no words — just a melody, passed down from her mother, who was a nurse. The melody is in a minor key but resolves to major on the last phrase.
entries.lyrics:
[NO WORDS — HUMMED MELODY]

Transcription: E-G-A, E-G-A, F-E-D, C-D-E. / Repeat. / Final phrase: C-D-E-F-G-A-B, resolve to C major.

The Therapist notes that patients who hear this lullaby before surgery report lower anxiety and faster recovery. The Surgeon says it's just a song. The patients say it's the only gentle thing in the bunker.

entries.title: The Salt Freeholders' March
entries.performance_context: Sung by the Salt Freeholders when walking between claim posts. The rhythm matches a walking pace. The lyrics are a statement of territorial claim — sung loudly, so anyone within earshot knows the land is occupied.
entries.lyrics:
This ridge is ours, this water's ours, / This salt is ours beneath the ground. / We walked it first, we marked it plain, / We'll walk it still till we go down.

The Brine Accord is signed in sweat, / The claim post stands, the tin plate shines. / No trespasser takes what we have earned, / No raider crosses these salt lines.

March on, march on, the Freeholders walk, / From ridge to creek, from creek to sea. / The salt is ours, the water's ours, / And we are free. And we are free.

entries.title: The Ash Falls Down
entries.performance_context: Sung by toddlers and young children in the nursery. Accompanied by hand gestures — raising hands above the head for 'ash falls,' covering eyes for 'can't see,' hugging self for 'warm inside.'
entries.lyrics:
The ash falls down, the ash falls down, / All over the bunker, all over the town. / It falls on the roof, it falls on the door, / It falls on the ground where we can't go anymore.

But we're warm inside, we're warm inside, / The walls keep the cold and the ash outside. / The lights go on, the water runs, / We're safe and warm until the sun.

The ash falls down but we don't care, / We've got each other and we've got air. / The ash falls down and we stay here, / Safe and warm until the year.

entries.title: The Cartographer's Song
entries.performance_context: Attributed to Bram Ostrowski, the mapmaker. Sung by couriers and scouts when walking long routes. The lyrics describe landmarks in order — a mnemonic device for navigation as much as a song.
entries.lyrics:
From the Toll Gate head south by east, / Past the silo where the green light ceased. / Cross the creek at the broken bridge, / Climb the ridge to the western ridge.

The geo-thermal vents steam white, / The arcology stands against the night. / The frozen barge lists in the ice, / The seed vault holds its cargo nice.

Forty kilometres, give or take, / Of broken road and frozen lake. / Walk the line, don't lose the track, / The map is true. Come safely back.

entries.title: Hymn of the Settling Dust
entries.performance_context: Sung at the annual Day of Remembrance — the anniversary of the first detonation. The entire bunker stands in silence for one minute, then sings this hymn in unison. The Priest leads. No one else speaks.
entries.lyrics:
The dust is settling, grain by grain. / The wind is dying, breath by breath. / The fire is cooling, year by year. / The earth is patient. We are less.

We built our towers. They fell. / We drew our borders. They burned. / We named our dead. They rest. / The dust remembers what we learned.

The dust is settling. Let it settle. / The ash is patient. Let it rest. / We are the ones who broke the world. / Let us be the ones who mend what's left.

The dust is settling. We are still here. / The ash is quiet. We endure. / The world is broken. We are whole. / The dust is settling. We endure.
